planting.note: Pot up nursery starts into a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss, orchid bark, and perlite; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater. Nepenthes rajah is a cool highland species from Borneo that needs cooler nights than most lowland Nepenthes and is considerably more demanding to grow well.

directions: Grow in a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss, orchid bark, and perlite in bright, filtered light with high humidity and cooler nights than typical lowland Nepenthes, watering only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rain water. Nepenthes rajah produces the largest pitchers of any carnivorous plant in the world, sometimes over a foot tall and capable of holding several pints of digestive fluid, occasionally even trapping small vertebrates like rodents in the wild in addition to its usual insect prey. Unlike vigorous, easy hybrids such as Miranda or Ventrata, it is a slow-growing, cool-highland species that struggles in typical warm home conditions and is best suited to an experienced grower with a terrarium or greenhouse that can maintain cooler, more humid conditions. Feed occasionally with a small live or dead insect if grown away from natural prey, and never use fertilizer in the soil.

directions: Grow in a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite in bright, filtered light with above-average humidity, watering only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rain water. Nepenthes ampullaria has an unusual growth habit among pitcher plants, producing dense clusters of small, rounded, urn-shaped ground pitchers directly along creeping stems rather than dangling singly from climbing vines, often carpeting the forest floor in its native Southeast Asian habitat. It also feeds more heavily on falling leaf litter than on captured insects, functioning partly as a detritivore rather than relying purely on live prey, which makes it somewhat more tolerant of lower light than many other Nepenthes species. Its clumping, spreading habit suits a wide, shallow container better than a hanging basket built for trailing vines. Feed occasionally with a small pinch of dried leaf litter or a dead insect if grown away from natural conditions.
